title: Using packages built on jlbind
text:
Source: vignettes/using-clients.qmd
jlbind lets R packages call Julia code compiled ahead of time into a shared library, without a Julia session. This vignette explains how that library works and how to use an R package built with jlbind. To add Julia functions to your own R package, see Get started with jlbind and Writing bindings. For how jlbind compares with other ways of calling Julia from R, see Performance.

title: Using packages built on jlbind
text:
How it works
Julia runs one runtime per process, with one compiled image, so the clients loaded in an R session (the R packages that use jlbind) share one compiled library. jlbind builds that library for each user, combining the Julia code of all installed clients. When you run install_library(), jlbind finds the installed clients, compiles their binding packages into one library, and saves it under tools::R_user_dir("jlbind", "cache"). Loading a client loads that library and connects the client to it.
A client is bound to a library built from the version of that client currently installed. If you update a package without rebuilding the library, its functions report that the library needs to be rebuilt.

title: Using packages built on jlbind
section: Using a package built on jlbind
text:
Using a package built on jlbind
You need Julia 1.13 or later to build the shared library.
After installing or updating an R package that uses jlbind, run:
jlbind::install_library()
The first build downloads and compiles the required Julia dependencies, so it may take a few minutes.






NoteRestart R after rebuilding a library that is already loaded



Julia cannot be restarted within an R session. If the old library has already been loaded, rebuilding it on disk does not replace the copy in memory. Restart R to use the new library.



If something doesn’t work correctly
If a package that uses jlbind doesn’t work, first check its status:
jlbind::check_bound("somepkg")
The most common causes are that the shared library hasn’t been built yet, or that the package was updated after the last build. For a full report, run:
jlbind::jlbind_sitrep()
It shows the Julia that install_library() would use (with its version, and whether it came from JULIA or the PATH), the library and what it was built from, each installed package that uses jlbind and whether the library is current for it, and the thread count. It works whether or not a library has loaded, and returns the same information invisibly as a list.
If the Julia installation used for the build has been removed or replaced, for example by a juliaup update, rebuild the library. install_library() rebuilds it when the Julia version differs from the one it was built with. If the version is the same, use force = TRUE:
jlbind::install_library(force = TRUE)
You can select the Julia installation to use by setting the JULIA environment variable or by passing julia = to install_library().
The library is compiled for the building machine’s CPU, and jlbind won’t load it on another. If one R library is used from computers with different CPUs, see CPU target.


Threads
Julia runs with one thread by default. To use multiple threads, set JULIA_NUM_THREADS before loading the first package that uses jlbind, for example in your .Renviron file:
JULIA_NUM_THREADS=auto # or a number, such as 4
The thread count is fixed when the library is loaded, so restart R after changing it. Each private library starts its own threads, as many as JULIA_NUM_THREADS says.

title: Using packages built on jlbind
text:
When clients conflict
All clients in the shared library use one set of Julia dependencies. By default, the build starts from the versions in the Manifest.toml of the first client that has one, and keeps them for the other clients where their [compat] bounds allow. Pass versions = "compat" to ignore the manifests and let Julia’s resolver choose versions from the clients’ [compat] bounds alone.
If a client’s [compat] bounds conflict with those of the clients listed before it by jlbind_clients(), the build leaves it out; check_bound() says which clients it conflicts with. You can then choose which clients to build the shared library from, give the conflicting client a private library (Linux and macOS), or build separate libraries for separate R sessions. Shared, private and separate libraries compares these and explains when to use each.

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Description
Finds the @rcall declarations in the package’s Julia binding package and writes R/jlbind-wrappers.R, with an R function for each that calls the compiled Julia function. Run this whenever you add or remove an @rcall, or change its arguments. @rcall shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Float64 = 0.0)::Float64 becomes shift <- function(x, by = 0.0) .External(.jlbind$.call, .jlbind$shift, x, by), where bind_client() puts the compiled function into .jlbind.

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Usage
update_entrypoints(path = ".")

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Arguments



path


Path to the package sources.

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Details
Defaults must be literal numbers, strings, true, false, missing (NA) or nothing (NULL), or vectors of these, such as [1, 2] (c(1, 2)) or Float64[] (numeric(0)). A function returning Nothing returns invisibly. To export or document a function, write roxygen comments (#') directly above its @rcall: they’re copied above the R function, so roxygen2 sees its signature. To add R code around a call, declare the Julia function with a jl_ prefix and write the R function yourself, calling the generated jl_ function.

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Value
Invisibly, a data frame of the entrypoints with the columns name, nargs, and the formals, args, invisible (whether it returns invisibly) and roxygen (the comments above its @rcall) of their R wrappers.

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Examples

# A package set up with use_jlbind() in a temporary directory
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "addpkg")
dir.create(pkg)
writeLines(
  c(
    "Package: addpkg",
    "Title: Demo",
    "Version: 0.1.0",
    "Description: Demo.",
    "License: MIT"
  ),
  file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION")
)
use_jlbind(pkg)
#> Created the binding package addpkgBindings in /tmp/RtmpuUMIY0/addpkg/inst/julia.
#> Wrote /tmp/RtmpuUMIY0/addpkg/R/jlbind-wrappers.R (1 entrypoints).

# Add an entrypoint to the binding package, before its closing `end`
file <- file.path(pkg, "inst/julia/src/addpkgBindings.jl")
code <- readLines(file)
last <- max(grep("^end", code))
code <- append(
  code,
  c(
    "add(x, y) = x + y",
    "@rcall add(x::Float64, y::Float64)::Float64",
    ""
  ),
  after = last - 1L
)
writeLines(code, file)

update_entrypoints(pkg)
#> Wrote /tmp/RtmpuUMIY0/addpkg/R/jlbind-wrappers.R (2 entrypoints).
writeLines(readLines(file.path(pkg, "R", "jlbind-wrappers.R")))
#> # Generated by jlbind::update_entrypoints(): do not edit by hand
#> 
#> # The entrypoints of the Julia binding package, which
#> # jlbind::bind_client() looks up in the compiled library and puts into
#> # `.jlbind` for the functions below.
#> .jlbind_module <- "addpkgBindings"
#> .jlbind_entries <- c(
#>   "hello",
#>   "add"
#> )
#> .jlbind <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
#> 
#> hello <- function(name) .External(.jlbind$.call, .jlbind$hello, name)
#> add <- function(x, y) .External(.jlbind$.call, .jlbind$add, x, y)

title: Build options
text:
Source: vignettes/build-options.qmd
This vignette covers the options for building a jlbind library, mostly for other computers: cluster nodes with different CPUs, or computers without Julia. Using packages built on jlbind covers the everyday use of install_library().

title: Build options
text:
Default options
jlbind compiles the library with these options, which keep it small and fast. Most users don’t need to change them.

text:
CPU target
Use cpu_target if one R library is used from computers with different CPUs, such as cluster nodes sharing a home directory:
jlbind::install_library(cpu_target = "generic")
This table compares the options on an x86-64 Linux computer (AMD Zen 4) with Julia 1.14. Library size is the compiled library file for CausalStructures.jl, a package of graph algorithms; the Julia runtime it loads adds about 6 MB. Run times are relative to "native", so 2× takes twice as long. Graph code is CausalStructures.jl, and the other columns are small numeric kernels. Results will differ for other packages and computers. The benchmark code is in the jlbind repository.

The several targets measured here are those of Julia’s own system image, which keep numeric code fast across x86-64 CPUs:

JULIA_CPU_TARGET=generic

title: Build options
text:
Julia arguments
For advanced use, julia_args passes extra options to Julia when it compiles the library, such as "-O3", or "-g1" to keep the debug info that jlbind removes with -g0. You can also set them in JLBIND_JULIA_ARGS, separated by spaces. They can’t change the options jlbind relies on: --trim, --output-* and --compile-ccallable.

title: Build options
text:
Bundled runtimes
A library loads the runtime of the Julia that built it, so that Julia stays installed. With bundle = TRUE, jlbind copies Julia’s runtime next to the library, into jlbind-bundle/, using JuliaC’s --bundle, so that it runs on a computer without Julia:
jlbind::build_library(
  c("pkgA", "pkgB"),
  "~/jlbind/bundle",
  cpu_target = "generic",
  bundle = TRUE
)
Give the users the whole directory, built on the same operating system and CPU architecture as theirs. Then they set JLBIND_LIBRARY to the library in it before loading the clients.
A private library is a bundle too: it has its own copy of the runtime, whose symbols JuliaC renames (--privatize) so that it loads alongside other Julia runtimes. So it also runs without Julia, and takes the same disk space as a bundle.

Bundle sizes
A bundle holds the runtime libraries Julia declares it needs, and those of the standard libraries in the packages’ Julia environment. With Julia 1.14 or later, jlbind leaves out the libraries JuliaC copies for standard libraries that nothing in the image depends on, such as OpenBLAS (36 MB) when no package depends on LinearAlgebra or OpenBLAS_jll. Any dependency that declares LinearAlgebra keeps OpenBLAS in the bundle, whether or not the compiled code calls BLAS; when it is unused, remove it by hand. These sizes are for the whole directory, with cpu_target = "generic" on the computer above, for CausalStructures.jl (whose dependencies declare LinearAlgebra, while its compiled code runs without BLAS) and for a tiny package:

Removing more by hand
To get the last row, delete jlbind-bundle/share, and everything in jlbind-bundle/lib and jlbind-bundle/lib/julia except libjulia, libjulia-internal, libunwind, libz, libzstd, libatomic, libgcc_s and libopenlibm, then run strip on the library. In a private library, under tools::R_user_dir("jlbind", "cache"), the names of libjulia and libjulia-internal start with the library’s salt, such as jl0f5ce2_. A call that needs a removed library gives an error that names it. Test every package after removing anything.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Source: vignettes/jlbind.qmd
jlbind lets an R package call Julia code without starting a Julia session. The Julia code is compiled ahead of time into a shared library, and R calls it through native .External() calls.
You need Julia 1.13 or later, and devtools for the development workflow below.
We will refer to an R package that uses jlbind as a client.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Set up your package
From your R package’s directory, run:
jlbind::use_jlbind()
devtools::document()
This adds everything your package needs to talk to Julia, including a Julia binding package in inst/julia/. For a package called mypkg, its main file is inst/julia/src/mypkgBindings.jl, and it comes with one example function:
module mypkgBindings

using JLBind

hello(name) = "Hello, " * name * ", from Julia!"

@rcall hello(name::String)::String

end # module mypkgBindings
@rcall declares a Julia function that R can call, along with its argument and return types. Every argument and the return value need a type: the types decide how values are converted between R and Julia (see Types). The JLBind reference lists everything else JLBind provides.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Try the example
use_jlbind() has already generated the R function for hello(), so all that’s left is to compile the Julia code and load your package:
jlbind::build_library()
devtools::load_all()
The first build downloads and compiles Julia dependencies, so it may take a few minutes. Then call it like any R function:
hello("world")
#> [1] "Hello, world, from Julia!"

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Add your own function
Adding a function takes three steps.

1. Declare it in Julia
Inside the module in the binding package, write the function and declare it with @rcall. Defaults in the declaration become R defaults:
shift(x, by) = x .+ by

@rcall shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Float64 = 1.0)::Vector{Float64}


2. Generate its R function
jlbind::update_entrypoints()
This adds shift() to R/jlbind-wrappers.R:
shift <- function(x, by = 1.0) .External(.jlbind$.call, .jlbind$shift, x, by)






NoteWhat update_entrypoints() generates





R/jlbind-wrappers.R, which you shouldn’t edit by hand, also lists the declarations:
.jlbind_module <- "mypkgBindings"
.jlbind_entries <- c(
  "hello",
  "shift"
)
.jlbind <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
When your package loads, jlbind::bind_client() looks up each entry in the compiled library, shift as jlbind13_mypkgBindings_shift1, the function @rcall exports, and puts it into .jlbind. Calls go through .jlbind$.call, a routine in jlbind that turns a Julia error into an R error. If the R functions are out of date with the Julia code, as when you change an @rcall without running update_entrypoints(), calling one with the wrong number of arguments gives an error.





3. Restart R and load your package
A library that has loaded can’t be replaced, so restart R first. devtools::load_all() then rebuilds the library, since your Julia code changed. If you forget, devtools::load_all() warns that the development library is out of date and tells you to restart R.
Repeat these steps as you develop. If you only change the body of a Julia function, you can skip step 2.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Export your functions
To export or document a generated function, write roxygen comments directly above its @rcall:
#' Shift a vector
#'
#' @param x A numeric vector.
#' @param by The amount to shift by.
#' @export
@rcall shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Float64 = 1.0)::Vector{Float64}
update_entrypoints() copies them above shift() in R/jlbind-wrappers.R, so roxygen2 reads the function’s signature from there. To share a help page, use #' @rdname above the @rcall and write the page itself in R/, on NULL.
To add R code around a call, declare the Julia function with a jl_ prefix, e.g. @rcall jl_shift(...), and write shift() yourself, calling jl_shift().

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Share your package
Clients share one Julia runtime in an R process, so jlbind compiles the Julia code of all installed clients into one library on each user’s machine. Tell your users, for example in your README, to run this after installing your package:
jlbind::install_library()
Your package must also install and pass R CMD check without Julia, as on CRAN. In tests, skip anything that needs the library:
skip_if_not(jlbind::is_bound("mypkg"))
In examples, use roxygen’s @examplesIf:
#' @examplesIf jlbind::is_bound("mypkg")
#' x <- my_function(1:3)
#' x
Then run jlbind::use_jlbind_ci() to check your package both with and without Julia on GitHub Actions.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Next steps

Writing bindings covers what you’ll likely need next: the types R and Julia can exchange, keeping Julia objects in R, errors, the compilation constraints on your Julia code, and development libraries, including how to pin Julia dependency versions.
Using packages built on jlbind describes what your users see, including threads, how clients share Julia dependencies, and what users can do when clients conflict.
hellojl and counterjl are small, complete clients used in jlbind’s tests, and are good examples to learn from.

title: Check a package with its Julia code on GitHub Actions

Description
Writes a GitHub Actions workflow that checks the package with and without Julia. With Julia, it runs R CMD check on Linux and Windows after compiling the package’s Julia code with build_library(), so tests and examples that need the library run. Without Julia, it checks the package once on Linux, as CRAN does, where those tests and examples must be skipped. The workflow is written to .github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml.

Description
Lists the installed packages that install_library() will compile. A package uses jlbind if its DESCRIPTION has a Config/jlbind field. If a package is installed in more than one library, the copy that library() would load is the one listed.

A data frame with one row per package and the columns package, version, module (the name of its Julia binding package), path (where the binding package is), trim (FALSE if it sets Config/jlbind/trim: false) and hash (a hash of the binding package’s files, which the library records to tell when it is out of date).

Examples

Description
Compiles the Julia code of every installed package that uses jlbind into one shared library, stored in tools::R_user_dir("jlbind", "cache"). Run this after you install or update one of those packages. You need Julia 1.13 or later. The first build downloads and compiles the Julia dependencies, which can take a few minutes.

title: Build the Julia library
text:
Usage
install_library(
  packages = NULL,
  julia = NULL,
  ask = interactive(),
  force = FALSE,
  versions = c("manifest", "compat"),
  develop = NULL,
  cpu_target = NULL,
  julia_args = NULL,
  bundle = FALSE,
  private = NULL
)

title: Build the Julia library
text:
Arguments



packages


Names of the installed packages to build. By default, every package listed by jlbind_clients(). The others aren’t bound.




julia


Path to the julia executable. By default, the JULIA environment variable, or julia on the PATH.




ask


If TRUE, ask before building. Defaults to interactive().




force


If TRUE, rebuild even if the library is up to date. Always on with versions = "compat" or develop.




versions


Where the Julia dependency versions come from. "manifest" keeps the versions in the first package’s Manifest.toml where the other packages’ [compat] bounds allow. "compat" ignores the manifests and lets Julia’s resolver choose versions from the [compat] bounds alone.




develop


Paths to local Julia packages to use instead of their released versions.




cpu_target


The CPUs to compile for, as Julia’s --cpu-target. By default, JULIA_CPU_TARGET, or "native". "generic" runs on any CPU, but numeric code can be slower.




julia_args


For advanced use: extra Julia command-line options for compiling the library, such as "-O3". jlbind passes -g0 (no debug info), which these can override (e.g. "-g1"), but not the options it relies on: --trim, --output-* and --compile-ccallable. By default, JLBIND_JULIA_ARGS split at spaces.




bundle


If TRUE, copy the Julia runtime next to the shared library, so that it runs without Julia installed. This makes the library much larger, and is only useful for giving a library to people without Julia, who set JLBIND_LIBRARY to it. They also need a cpu_target other than "native". See vignette("build-options", "jlbind").




private


Names of packages among packages to give a library of their own, with a private Julia runtime, on Linux and macOS. By default, the packages given one by an earlier build. character() puts every package in the shared library.

title: Build the Julia library
text:
Details
All packages in the shared library share one Julia environment. By default, the dependencies get the versions in the first package’s Manifest.toml. If two packages conflict, the one listed later by jlbind_clients() is left out, and check_bound() says why. To use it anyway, give it a library of its own with private, which has its own copy of the Julia runtime and takes more disk space and memory, or build it into a separate library with build_library() for separate R sessions. See vignette("libraries", "jlbind") for how these compare.
A library is rebuilt only if it is out of date: built from other versions of the packages or their Julia code, by another version of jlbind or Julia, or with other options. If a library is already loaded, restart R to use the new one.
The library is compiled for this computer’s CPU, and jlbind won’t load it on another. If one R library is used from computers with different CPUs, as on a cluster, use cpu_target = "generic", or name CPUs they all support, such as "x86-64-v3". See vignette("build-options", "jlbind") for how these compare.

# Only two of the installed packages

# For an R library shared by computers with different CPUs
install_library(cpu_target = "generic")

# pkgB in a library of its own, as its Julia dependencies conflict with
# those of pkgA

title: Shared, private and separate libraries
text:
Source: vignettes/libraries.qmd
By default, install_library() compiles every installed client into one shared library. All clients in a library share one Julia environment, so when their [compat] bounds conflict, the build leaves the later ones out (see When clients conflict). Such a client can instead get a private library of its own, or go into a separate library that you select for the R sessions that use it. This vignette compares the three.
The overhead comes on top of each client’s compiled code, which every layout holds (about 9 MB for CausalStructures.jl; see Bundle sizes). A private library’s copy of the runtime grows with the standard libraries its dependencies use, to 76 MB for CausalStructures.jl, whose dependencies need OpenBLAS. With private or separate libraries, a dependency that several clients share is compiled into each of their libraries. Thus, we recommend you to use the default with shared libraries, unless impossible due to conflicts.

title: Shared, private and separate libraries
text:
The shared library
install_library() stores the shared library under tools::R_user_dir("jlbind", "cache") and rebuilds it whenever a client or the Julia version changes. It uses the runtime of the Julia that built it, so it is small, and all clients share one Julia heap, one set of threads and each other’s Julia objects. Each build compiles every client, and a client that conflicts with those before it is left out. To choose which clients to build it from, and in which order to resolve them, name them:
jlbind::install_library(packages = c("pkgA", "pkgC"))

title: Shared, private and separate libraries
text:
Private libraries
On Linux and macOS1, a client can get a library of its own:
jlbind::install_library(private = "pkgB")
This builds the shared library from the other clients, and a library for pkgB with its dependencies resolved for it alone. The private library has its own copy of the Julia runtime, with its symbols renamed (JuliaC’s --privatize), so it loads alongside the shared library and any other private ones, and pkgB works in the same R session as the clients it conflicts with. Later builds keep it, so install_library() rebuilds both. To put every client back into the shared library, pass private = character().
The runtime copy makes the library a bundle, so it runs without Julia installed. It takes disk space, and in each session its own memory and JULIA_NUM_THREADS threads. Julia objects that pkgB returns work with the functions of pkgB only.

title: Shared, private and separate libraries
text:
Separate libraries
Clients used in different R sessions can each have a library, built with build_library():
jlbind::build_library("pkgA", "~/jlbind/pkgA")
jlbind::build_library(c("pkgB", "pkgC"), "~/jlbind/pkgBC")
Set JLBIND_LIBRARY before the first client loads to select the library for a session, or in a project’s .Renviron for every session in that project:
# jlbind.dll on Windows, jlbind.dylib on macOS
Sys.setenv(JLBIND_LIBRARY = "~/jlbind/pkgA/jlbind.so")
library(pkgA)
Every client in that session then binds to this library, in place of the shared and private ones. A separate library is as small as the shared one, but you rebuild it yourself: after updating one of its clients, run build_library() again (check_bound() reports when it’s needed).

JuliaC gives a library a private Julia runtime on Linux and macOS. Windows support is in progress in JuliaC.jl#151.↩︎

Description
Prints a report to run when a package that uses jlbind doesn’t work. It shows the Julia that builds the libraries, the shared library that is loaded (or would be) and what it was built from, any private libraries (see private in install_library()), the installed packages that use jlbind and whether their library is current for each, and the Julia thread count. It also works before a library has loaded.

Usage
jlbind_sitrep(julia = NULL)

title: Report on the jlbind setup
text:
Arguments



julia


Path to the julia executable. By default, the JULIA environment variable, or julia on the PATH.

title: Report on the jlbind setup
text:
Value
Invisibly, a list with:


julia: a list with path (NA if Julia was not found), source ("argument", "JULIA" or "PATH"), version (NA if it could not be run) and ok (whether it is Julia 1.13 or later).


library: the shared library, a list with path, how ("loaded", "failed to load", "JLBIND_LIBRARY" or "default"), exists, build (how it was built: the jlbind and Julia versions, when, whether it is trimmed, the CPU target and the CPU it was built on, any extra Julia arguments, whether it is a bundle and the salt of a private runtime, or NULL), problems (why it should be rebuilt or cannot load; empty if none) and objects (how many Julia objects R holds references to, or NULL if it isn’t loaded).


private: the private libraries packages use, each a list like library, with how "loaded", "failed to load" or "private".


clients: a data frame with one row per package that uses jlbind or that a library was built for, with the columns package, version (installed), built (the version in its library), status ("ok", "left out", "not in the library", "built for version <v>", "Julia code changed" or "not installed"), bound and library (the path of its library).


threads: a list with count (from JULIA_NUM_THREADS, in each library; NA for "auto", the CPU threads available) and fixed (TRUE once a library is loaded, after which the count cannot change).

text:
Source: .github/CONTRIBUTING.md

Thanks for helping out! This page covers what you need to work on jlbind itself.
You may use LLMs, but please write issue and PR descriptions in your own words. If you submit a PR, you should understand the code you’re contributing.


The tests that compile a library are slow and skipped unless you opt in with environment variables:







Variable
Runs




JLBIND_TEST_BUILD=true

julia --project=inst/julia/JLBind -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.test()'
On Linux, R may fail to start inside Julia without R_HOME/lib on the library path, and exit without printing why. Run the tests with LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$(R RHOME)/lib" set.

text:
Source: vignettes/technical-details.qmd
This vignette covers what Get started with jlbind leaves out, so read that first.

title: Writing bindings
text:
One library for all clients
jlbind compiles Julia code with JuliaC.jl. Clients share one library and one Julia runtime, so your client shares Julia dependency versions with every other client the user has installed. Keep your [compat] bounds as wide as your code allows, so that it resolves alongside them.
When clients conflict, users can choose between them, give one a private library, or use separate libraries. A private library has its own copy of the Julia runtime, which takes disk space and memory.

title: Writing bindings
text:
What use_jlbind() adds

inst/julia/, containing a Julia binding package named after the R package with a Bindings suffix (for example, MyPkgBindings), including an example function.
R/jlbind-wrappers.R, with an R function for each Julia function the binding package declares.
An .onLoad() in R/zzz.R that calls jlbind::bind_client().
The Config/jlbind, Imports: jlbind and SystemRequirements: Julia (>= 1.13) fields in DESCRIPTION.
A .jlbind/ directory for development builds, added to .Rbuildignore and .gitignore.

If your package already defines .onLoad(), add jlbind::bind_client(pkgname) to the existing function yourself.






ImportantGive the Julia binding package a unique name



All clients are compiled into one library, so binding package names must be unique across all jlbind clients. The default, the R package name with a Bindings suffix, ensures this.

title: Writing bindings
text:
Writing @rcall declarations
The binding package is an ordinary Julia package. Add its dependencies with Pkg, from your package’s directory, and import them as usual:
julia --project=inst/julia -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.add("SomePackage")'






ImportantWrite @rcall declarations literally at the top level



jlbind finds @rcall declarations by scanning the source files, not by running them, so write them literally at the top level of the module.



Default values
A default in a declaration becomes the default of the generated R function. For example,
@rcall summarise(x::Vector{Float64}, probs::Vector{Float64} = [0.25, 0.75],
                 na::Union{Missing,Float64} = missing)::Vector{Float64}
generates
summarise <- function(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), na = NA) ...
A default can be any of these:



Julia default
R default




A literal number or string
The same literal


true, false
TRUE, FALSE


missing
NA


nothing
NULL


[1, 2], Float64[1, 2]
c(1, 2)


["a", missing]
c("a", NA)


Float64[], String[], …
numeric(0), character(0), …



An empty vector names its element type, as in Int32[] or Bool[].

title: Writing bindings
text:
Development libraries
By default, build_library() writes the library to .jlbind/ in your package’s source directory. When you load the package with devtools::load_all(), jlbind uses this development library instead of the one created by install_library(). Once .jlbind/ exists, devtools::load_all() rebuilds it when your binding package’s files or your package’s version have changed since it was built.






NoteThe development library is only used when your package loads first



A library that has loaded cannot be replaced, so the .jlbind/ library is used only if your package is the first jlbind client loaded in the R session. On Linux and macOS, build_library(private = TRUE) gives the development library its own copy of the Julia runtime, so it loads alongside the shared library whatever the order.


If you need to use a library stored elsewhere, set the JLBIND_LIBRARY environment variable to its path before loading the package.
You can also test against an unreleased version of a Julia dependency by providing a local checkout through develop:
jlbind::build_library(develop = "~/dev/SomePackage.jl")






TipPin the dependency versions



Include a Manifest.toml next to the binding package’s Project.toml with the Julia dependency versions known to compile with your package. CRAN’s policy asks that downloaded libraries be a fixed version rather than the latest.
The build uses the manifest of only the first client that has one (see When clients conflict), so keep your [compat] bounds accurate too.

Int64 results: these become doubles, since R’s integers have 32 bits. Return Int32 for an R integer.
Dates: to use Date or DateTime, add the Dates standard library to the binding package’s dependencies.
Lists: if one element of a list can’t be converted, the error says which. For example, passing list(c(1, 2), "a") as a Vector{Vector{Float64}} gives the error element 2: expected a numeric vector.



Data frames
To take or return a data frame, wrap the columns in an RDataFrame. Its type lists the column names and the type of each column, so a type alias keeps signatures short:
const Sales = RDataFrame{(:group, :amount),Tuple{Vector{String},Vector{Float64}}}
const Summary = RDataFrame{(:group, :mean),Tuple{Vector{String},Vector{Float64}}}

function summarise(df)
    gs = sort(unique(df.group))
    means = [sum(df.amount[df.group .== g]) / count(==(g), df.group) for g in gs]
    return RDataFrame((group = gs, mean = means))
end

@rcall summarise(df::Sales)::Summary
summarise(data.frame(group = c("a", "b", "a"), amount = c(1, 2, 3)))
#>   group mean
#> 1     a    2
#> 2     b    2
An RDataFrame argument:

Must be a data frame (a tibble works too) with exactly the declared columns, in any order. If the data frame has other columns, select the ones you need in the R wrapper: summarise(df[c("group", "amount")]).
Has its columns as properties (df.group), and NamedTuple(df) returns them as a named tuple.
Converts each column by the usual rules, so a factor column arrives as strings, and a Vector{Union{Missing,Float64}} column allows NA.

Returning columns of different lengths is an error.
If you don’t need a data frame on the Julia side, a NamedTuple argument also accepts one, as a named tuple of its columns. It must have exactly the names of its fields, in any order.


Large vectors
Other conversions copy, so a function given a large vector it only reads can take an RVector{Float64} (or RVector{Int32}, RVector{UInt8}). That is an AbstractVector viewing R’s memory, without checking for NA. It is valid only until the call returns, so don’t store it.


Your own types
JLBind is jlbind’s own Julia package, which every binding package depends on, so write JLBind.foo as it is rather than with the name of your package.
A binding package can support additional types by defining methods for JLBind.from_sexp(::Type{T}, x::SEXP) and JLBind.to_sexp(x::T). JLBind also provides helpers for building R objects directly, such as JLBind.data_frame() for a data frame whose columns are not known when the library is compiled, and JLBind.alloc() and JLBind.alloc_matrix() for a vector or matrix to fill in place, without a copy in Julia first. The JLBind reference documents all of them.






WarningAvoid type piracy



By default, every client is compiled into the same library, so a pirated method of a JLBind function changes it for every client, and two clients pirating the same method fail to compile together. To convert a type you don’t own, wrap it in your own struct or open an issue to add it to JLBind.




Julia objects in R
Sometimes an object is better kept in Julia: it has no natural R equivalent, or it is large, such as a fitted model, and converting it on every call would be slow. You can pass such objects by reference using RRef{T}. R receives an external pointer to the Julia object, allowing it to be reused across calls. The object is released when R garbage-collects the reference, and jlbind::object_count() counts the objects R holds, to check that a package doesn’t leak them.
For example, define a mutable Julia object and expose functions that operate on it (the counterjl test client is a complete version of this):
mutable struct Counter
    n::Int64
end

JLBind.r_class(::Type{Counter}) = "counter"

new_counter(start) = Counter(start)
increment(c, by) = (c.n += by; c.n)

@rcall new_counter(start::Int64)::RRef{Counter}
@rcall increment(c::RRef{Counter}, by::Int64)::Int64
From R, you can create a counter and update it across calls:
counter <- new_counter(0)
class(counter)
#> [1] "counter"

increment(counter, 2)
#> [1] 2
r_class() sets the R class of the external pointer, so your package can define methods such as print() for it. An argument declared as RRef{Counter} also checks that the reference points to a Counter, rather than accepting an arbitrary Julia object. A reference works with the library that made it, so with a client in a private library, its references work with that client’s functions only.


Saving Julia objects
R writes an external pointer as a null pointer, so by default a reference does not survive saveRDS(), save(), serialize(), or being sent to a parallel worker; using it afterwards gives an error. To make a type savable, you need to do two things.
In Julia, define JLBind.r_saved_by(), which names your R package, and JLBind.r_restore(), which rebuilds the object from the saved data:
JLBind.r_saved_by(::Type{Counter}) = "mypackage"
JLBind.r_restore(::Type{Counter}, state::SEXP) =
    Counter(from_sexp(NamedTuple{(:n,),Tuple{Int64}}, state).n)

counter_value(c) = c.n

@rcall counter_value(c::RRef{Counter})::Int64
In R, define .jlbind_saved_state(), which returns that data as a list of plain R values. It is internal, so don’t export it. If your package has several savable types, branch on the class of x:
.jlbind_saved_state <- function(x) {
  list(n = counter_value(x))
}
The first call that uses a loaded object rebuilds it, which needs the compiled library.
.jlbind_saved_state() only runs when saving, through an ALTREP vector in the reference’s jlbind_state attribute. Creating this vector adds about 400 ns to each new reference.

title: Writing bindings
text:
Errors
If a function called through @rcall throws a Julia exception, jlbind turns it into an R error. The messages from ArgumentError, ErrorException, DimensionMismatch, OverflowError, and AssertionError are passed through. Other exceptions are summarized.

title: Writing bindings
text:
Compilation constraints (trimming)
By default, jlbind compiles the shared library with juliac --trim=safe. This keeps the compiled image small by including only code reachable from the functions exposed through @rcall. It also requires calls to be resolvable at compile time.
If your package cannot be compiled with trimming, add the following field to DESCRIPTION:
Config/jlbind/trim: false






Warning



An untrimmed library includes the full Julia system image and is much larger, so avoid it if you can.



Abstract types
With trimming, a common source of compilation errors is a function that accepts several concrete types through an abstract RRef. Suppose your binding package works with shapes:


Shape types and their areas

abstract type Shape end

struct Circle <: Shape
    radius::Float64
end
struct Square <: Shape
    side::Float64
end
struct Rectangle <: Shape
    width::Float64
    height::Float64
end
struct Triangle <: Shape
    base::Float64
    height::Float64
end

JLBind.r_class(::Type{<:Shape}) = "shape"

area(s::Circle) = pi * s.radius^2
area(s::Square) = s.side^2
area(s::Rectangle) = s.width * s.height
area(s::Triangle) = s.base * s.height / 2

An entrypoint that takes an RRef{Shape} knows only that its argument is some Shape. If it simply calls area(s), the compiler cannot tell which of the four methods that call reaches, and the build fails with an error such as:
Verifier error #1: unresolved call from statement area(s::Shape)::Any
The solution is to take the argument with @nospecialize and branch on the concrete types, making the call inside each branch, where the type is known. @narrow s (A, B, ...) expr does that: it evaluates expr with s narrowed to whichever of the listed types it is (see its reference):
circle(radius) = Circle(radius)
square(side) = Square(side)
rectangle(width, height) = Rectangle(width, height)
triangle(base, height) = Triangle(base, height)
shape_area(@nospecialize(s::Shape)) =
    @narrow s (Circle, Square, Rectangle, Triangle) area(s)
scaled_area(@nospecialize(s::Shape), factor::Float64) =
    @narrow s (Circle, Square, Rectangle, Triangle) factor^2 * area(s)

@rcall circle(radius::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall square(side::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall rectangle(width::Float64, height::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall triangle(base::Float64, height::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall shape_area(shape::RRef{Shape})::Float64
@rcall scaled_area(shape::RRef{Shape}, factor::Float64)::Float64
Every shape can then be passed to the same generated R functions:
shapes <- list(circle(1), square(2), rectangle(2, 3), triangle(2, 3))
vapply(shapes, shape_area, numeric(1))
#> [1] 3.141593 4.000000 6.000000 3.000000

scaled_area(square(2), 3)
#> [1] 36
A shape of a type that isn’t listed gives the error expected Circle, Square, Rectangle or Triangle; a fourth argument to @narrow is evaluated instead, to give another error or a default. List only the types the call has methods for.
Without @nospecialize, Julia compiles a separate shape_area for each concrete shape, and the call into it from the entrypoint can’t be resolved, for the same reason as area(s). A function that receives the shape and passes it on needs @nospecialize too.
If a hierarchy has only a few types, some alternatives to @nospecialize are:

Declare a separate entrypoint for each concrete type (RRef{Circle},RRef{Square}, …) and choose between them in R.
Use a small Union such as RRef{Union{Circle,Square}}, which Julia resolves by checking each member in turn.



Other calls that don’t compile
The same rule, that every call must resolve when the library is compiled, rules out a few common patterns:

Splatting a vector, as in f(xs...) for xs::Vector: the number of arguments is only known at run time. Call a method that takes the vector, or call f once per element if that gives the same result.
Names of abstract types, as in nameof(typeof(x)) where x is only known to be some Shape. Use @narrow to give each type its name.
Types as keyword arguments, as in f(; type = T): the keyword arguments are stored in a NamedTuple whose field is only a DataType. Pass the type positionally, or call the keyword form with @inline where T is a constant.

Optional arguments are not a problem: @rcall calls the function in a separate branch for nothing (or missing) and for a value of each argument declared as a Union{Nothing,T} (or Union{Missing,T}), so each call has concrete types. This needs the Union written out in the declaration, not an alias for it.

title: Build a Julia library from specific packages
text:
Description
Like install_library(), but compiles only packages and writes the library to out, for package development. By default, it builds the package in the working directory into its .jlbind/ directory, which devtools::load_all() then uses instead of the library from install_library(). To use a library written elsewhere, set JLBIND_LIBRARY to its path before loading the package.

title: Build a Julia library from specific packages
text:
Usage
build_library(
  packages = ".",
  out = NULL,
  julia = NULL,
  versions = c("manifest", "compat"),
  develop = NULL,
  cpu_target = NULL,
  julia_args = NULL,
  bundle = FALSE,
  private = FALSE
)

title: Build a Julia library from specific packages
text:
Arguments



packages


Paths to package sources or installed packages, or names of installed packages. An entry containing a / (or \ on Windows), or that is "." or "..", is a path; any other is a package name, so write "./mypkg" for the sources in the mypkg directory.




out


Directory to write the library to. Defaults to .jlbind/ in the sources of packages, which must then be a single path.




julia


Path to the julia executable. By default, the JULIA environment variable, or julia on the PATH.




versions


Where the Julia dependency versions come from. "manifest" keeps the versions in the first package’s Manifest.toml where the other packages’ [compat] bounds allow. "compat" ignores the manifests and lets Julia’s resolver choose versions from the [compat] bounds alone.




develop


Paths to local Julia packages to use instead of their released versions.




cpu_target


The CPUs to compile for, as Julia’s --cpu-target. By default, JULIA_CPU_TARGET, or "native". "generic" runs on any CPU, but numeric code can be slower.




julia_args


For advanced use: extra Julia command-line options for compiling the library, such as "-O3". jlbind passes -g0 (no debug info), which these can override (e.g. "-g1"), but not the options it relies on: --trim, --output-* and --compile-ccallable. By default, JLBIND_JULIA_ARGS split at spaces.




bundle


If TRUE, copy the Julia runtime next to the shared library, so that it runs without Julia installed. This makes the library much larger, and is only useful for giving a library to people without Julia, who set JLBIND_LIBRARY to it. They also need a cpu_target other than "native". See vignette("build-options", "jlbind").




private


If TRUE, give the library a private Julia runtime, as private does in install_library(). The library then loads alongside the shared one, and the packages built into it bind to it.

text:
Value
The path to the library, invisibly.

# In the sources of a package that uses jlbind
build_library()
devtools::load_all()

# Several packages, used through JLBIND_LIBRARY
lib <- build_library(c("pkg1", "pkg2"), "jlbind-lib")
Sys.setenv(JLBIND_LIBRARY = lib)

title: Performance
text:
Source: vignettes/articles/performance.qmd
jlbind calls Julia code that was compiled ahead of time, through one .External() per function. The alternatives, JuliaCall and JuliaConnectoR, run Julia itself: JuliaCall embeds a Julia session in the R process, and JuliaConnectoR starts one in a separate process and talks to it over a socket. This article compares the three on the same Julia functions.
In short, on this machine, jlbind is ready to use 105 to 137 times sooner, and a call costs 0.912 µs rather than 8.76 µs (JuliaCall) or 207 µs (JuliaConnectoR).

title: Performance
text:
The benchmarks
The functions are those of benchjl, a minimal jlbind client kept next to the benchmark script:
greet(name) = "Hello, " * name * "!"
shift(x, by) = x .+ by
jlbind calls them through benchjl, compiled into a jlbind library. JuliaCall and JuliaConnectoR evaluate the same definitions and call them with julia_call() and juliaFun(). Each interface runs in fresh R processes, since jlbind and JuliaCall can’t share one.

Startup: the median time from loading the package to the result of the first call, greet("world"), in a new R process (R’s own startup excluded), over 10 repetitions.
Call overhead: the median time of greet("world"), a string in and a string out, after the first call.
Data transfer: the median time of shift(x, 1) for numeric vectors x of length 10 to 107, which copies x to Julia and the result back.

Each table shows the median time for each interface and, in parentheses, how many times jlbind’s median it is.

Startup





jlbind
JuliaCall

28.8 ms
3.94 s (137×)
3.02 s (105×)





For jlbind, startup is loading the compiled library and binding the package’s routines. JuliaCall and JuliaConnectoR start Julia, and compile each function the first time it is called. With a real Julia package instead of two one-line functions, the gap is usually larger: although Julia caches a package’s precompiled code across sessions, each new session still loads it and compiles whatever the cache doesn’t cover.

Call overhead





jlbind
JuliaCall

207 µs (227×)





A jlbind call is an .External() call into jlbind’s C code, which calls the compiled library directly, where the arguments are converted with R’s C API. JuliaCall converts arguments and looks up the function at run time in the embedded session. JuliaConnectoR serializes the call to a separate Julia process and the result back, so each call costs a round trip.

title: jlbind
text:
Call Julia code from R without starting a Julia session.
jlbind compiles Julia code into a shared library with JuliaC.jl (by default with --trim=safe), and R calls it through R’s official C API. Thus, there is almost no overhead (see Performance).


# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("BjarkeHautop/jlbind")
Building the shared library requires Julia >= 1.13. Installing jlbind does not itself build the library.
Julia 1.14 or later is recommended: Julia 1.13 can compile a library that crashes as it loads. This happens when every compiled specialization of a method has a type parameter bounded by a Union (where {T<:Union{...}}): trimming then overwrites the image’s shared empty Memory{Any}. It is fixed in JuliaLang/julia#63664.



After installing or updating an R package that uses jlbind, build the shared library:
jlbind::install_library()
This compiles the Julia code of every installed package that uses jlbind and may take a few minutes. Run it again whenever you install or update one of them.
See Using packages built on jlbind for threads, troubleshooting and what to do when packages conflict, and Build options for CPU targets and libraries for computers without Julia.



Set up a package with jlbind::use_jlbind(), then declare the Julia functions R can call in the generated binding package under inst/julia/:
module MyPkgBindings

using JLBind

greet(name) = "Hello, " * name * "!"
@rcall greet(name::String)::String

end # module MyPkgBindings
Run jlbind::update_entrypoints(), which generates the R function greet(name) that calls it.
See Get started with jlbind for a walkthrough, and Writing bindings for types, errors and compilation constraints.




CausalStructures: causal graphs (DAGs, CPDAGs, PAGs, …) and identification, from CausalStructures.jl. Its binding package shows some advanced usage, such as:

R holds graphs of an abstract type (RRef{CausalGraph}), and each function branches on the concrete class (DAG, PAG, …) with @narrow.
Graphs survive saveRDS()/readRDS() via ALTREP (r_saved_by and r_restore).
Large results (edge lists, data frames) are built in place through R’s C API.

text:
Source: vignettes/articles/jlbind-reference.qmd
JLBind is the Julia package your binding package uses to talk to R. using JLBind gives you @rcall, @narrow, from_sexp, to_sexp, SEXP, RRef, RVector and RDataFrame; use the rest as JLBind.name.

title: JLBind reference
JLBind reference
JLBind reference
text:
Julia objects in R

RRef
RRef{T}
A Julia object that R holds by reference, for objects that are easier to keep in Julia than to convert:
new_counter(start) = Counter(start)
increment(c, by) = (c.n += by; c.n)

@rcall new_counter(start::Int64)::RRef{Counter}
@rcall increment(c::RRef{Counter}, by::Int64)::Int64
R gets an object of class r_class(T) that it can pass back to any entrypoint taking an RRef{T}, and a Vector{RRef{T}} is a list of them. The Julia object is freed once R no longer uses it. A reference that is saved and loaded again has lost its object, unless the type supports saving (see r_saved_by).
If T is abstract, take the argument with @nospecialize and call methods on it with @narrow.


r_class
r_class(T) -> String
The R class of references to Ts, "jlbind_ref" by default. Define a method to give them a class of their own, for methods such as print():
JLBind.r_class(::Type{Model}) = "mymodel"


r_saved_by
r_saved_by(T) -> Union{String,Nothing}
Return your package’s name to let references to Ts be saved with saveRDS() and the like. By default they can’t be: a reference that is saved and loaded again has lost its object.
Saving also needs an r_restore method, and an R function .jlbind_saved_state(x) in your package (it need not be exported) that returns a list to rebuild the object from:
JLBind.r_saved_by(::Type{Model}) = "mypackage"
JLBind.r_restore(::Type{Model}, state::SEXP) =
    Model(from_sexp(NamedTuple{(:weights,),Tuple{Vector{Float64}}}, state).weights)
.jlbind_saved_state <- function(x) list(weights = model_weights(x))
The object is rebuilt the first time a loaded reference is used. Supporting saving adds about 400 ns to creating each reference, and saveRDS(version = 2) can’t save one.


r_restore
r_restore(T, state::SEXP) -> T
Rebuild a T from the list .jlbind_saved_state() returned when it was saved (see r_saved_by). The list may come from an older version of your package, so check any version it records.


object_count
object_count() -> Int64
How many Julia objects R holds references to, to check that they are freed.

title: JLBind reference
JLBind reference
text:
Building R objects
To build a result yourself, without a copy, declare the entrypoint to return SEXP and use these, which call R’s C API directly. Most don’t check their arguments, so a wrong type or index crashes R instead of giving an error.

SEXP
SEXP
An R object, as R’s C API passes it. Declare an entrypoint to return SEXP to build its result yourself.


@R
@R(name)
A function or variable of R’s C API, for ccall or cglobal:
ccall(@R(Rf_xlength), Int, (SEXP,), x)


@r_global
@r_global(name)
The value of one of R’s global SEXP variables, such as @r_global(R_NaString).


nil
nil() -> SEXP
R’s NULL.


rtypeof, rlength
rtypeof(x::SEXP) -> Cint
rlength(x::SEXP) -> Int
The type of x (such as REALSXP), and its length.


NILSXP, LGLSXP, INTSXP, REALSXP, CPLXSXP, STRSXP, VECSXP, EXTPTRSXP, RAWSXP
NILSXP, LGLSXP, INTSXP, REALSXP, CPLXSXP, STRSXP, VECSXP, EXTPTRSXP, RAWSXP
R’s object types, as rtypeof returns them and alloc takes them: NULL, logical, integer, double, complex, character and raw vectors, a list, and an external pointer.


NA_INTEGER, NA_REAL
NA_INTEGER, NA_REAL
R’s NA in an integer or logical vector, and in a double vector.


protect, unprotect
protect(x::SEXP) -> x
unprotect(n)
Keep x from R’s garbage collector while you allocate other R objects, and release the last n objects protected, before returning. These are R’s PROTECT and UNPROTECT.


preserve, release
preserve(x::SEXP) -> x
release(x::SEXP)
Keep x alive across calls, until it is released.


alloc, alloc_matrix
alloc(t, n) -> SEXP
alloc_matrix(t, nrow, ncol) -> SEXP
A new R vector of type t and length n, or matrix of nrow rows and ncol columns, to fill in. protect it before allocating anything else.


mkchar
mkchar(s::Union{String,Symbol}) -> SEXP
An R string, the element of a character vector. Strings of symbols are cached, which makes returning many names faster.


string_elt, set_string_elt, vector_elt, set_vector_elt
string_elt(x::SEXP, i) -> SEXP
set_string_elt(x::SEXP, i, v::SEXP)
vector_elt(x::SEXP, i) -> SEXP
set_vector_elt(x::SEXP, i, v::SEXP)
Get and set element i of a character vector or list. Indices start at 0, as in C, and aren’t checked. Make an element of a character vector with mkchar.


real_ptr, int_ptr, logical_ptr, complex_ptr, raw_ptr
real_ptr(x::SEXP) -> Ptr{Float64}
int_ptr(x::SEXP) -> Ptr{Cint}
logical_ptr(x::SEXP) -> Ptr{Cint}
complex_ptr(x::SEXP) -> Ptr{ComplexF64}
raw_ptr(x::SEXP) -> Ptr{UInt8}
A pointer to the data of a double, integer, logical, complex or raw vector, to read with unsafe_load or fill with unsafe_store!. The type of x isn’t checked.


get_attrib, set_attrib
get_attrib(x::SEXP, name::SEXP) -> SEXP
set_attrib(x::SEXP, name::SEXP, value::SEXP)
Get and set the attribute name of x, where name is an R symbol such as @r_global(R_NamesSymbol). A missing attribute is NULL.


data_frame
data_frame(names::Vector{String}, columns::Vector{SEXP}) -> SEXP
An R data.frame of the R vectors columns, for columns whose types are only known at run time. Keep the columns protected until the call returns. When the types are known, return an RDataFrame instead.
